item.title: 'Forced labor' in Xinjiang's salmon industry, too? The New York Times has lost it: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 23:44:00
A salmon farm in Nilka County, Ili Kazak Autonomous Prefecture, Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. Photo: VCG In their attacks on Xinjiang-related issues, some Western media outlets are still deliberately presenting themselves as "objective and fair," but the signs of preconceived bias and a narrative assembled to fit a predetermined agenda are all too clear. Ultimately, no amount of smearing by US media can erase Xinjiang's economic and social development, nor can it stop people of all ethnic groups at the foot of the Tianshan Mountains from striving for a better life. Recently, The New York Times published a purported in-depth investigative report about the fish farming industry. The article adopts the posture of a "neutral" investigation, citing global research and evidence from multiple sources. It ranges from Peruvian fishing vessels and fishmeal processing plants to offshore aquaculture pens in Norway. Yet in the second half of the article, the focus takes a sharp turn toward the salmon industry in Northwest China's Xinjiang, devoting extensive coverage to recycling familiar allegations such as "forced labor." Read closely, the report reveals a familiar pattern: In their attacks on Xinjiang-related issues, some Western media outlets are still deliberately presenting themselves as "objective and fair," but the signs of preconceived bias and a narrative assembled to fit a predetermined agenda are all too clear. The report offers no evidence from firsthand interviews to support its claims about Xinjiang. Instead, it pieced together much of its narrative from vague attributions with phrases such as "claim," "accuse," and "most likely." By using documented problems in the seafood industry in other parts of the world to shape readers' perceptions in the first half, the article encourages them to assume that the claims made in the second half are equally well substantiated. However, the report provides no solid evidence that similar problems exist in Xinjiang, while packaging subjective speculation as so-called "investigative findings." Such journalistic practices run directly counter to the most basic standards of media credibility. Why are US media outlets willing to lose their credibility just to push out similar fake reports? The real aim, it would appear, is to lend support to Washington's unilateral sanctions targeting Xinjiang. From cotton and tomatoes to sunflower seeds and dumplings, and from solar photovoltaics to polysilicon, the pattern remains the same, with the focus now shifting to Xinjiang's cold-water fish industry: Any competitive industry that benefits Xinjiang's local communities is targeted with the "human rights" cudgel, as negative media coverage is paired with unilateral sanctions to suppress Chinese competitive industries and contain development in China's western regions. It's important to point out that what these sanctions are really aimed at is the employment and development rights of people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang. In fact, Xinjiang's salmon industry is a prime example of how local resources can be harnessed to turn geographical disadvantages into drivers of development. It is also a tangible achievement of China's campaign to develop its western regions in the new era. Nilka County in the Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture benefits from glacial meltwater flowing down from the Tianshan Mountains. The water remains cold and rich in dissolved oxygen throughout the year, and its excellent quality provides exceptional natural conditions for cold-water fish farming. Technologies such as automated feeding, underwater cleaning robots, and semi-closed recirculating aquaculture systems help minimize pollution, while uneaten feed and fish waste can be processed into organic fertilizer. The farming process emphasizes raising fish without medication and at low stocking densities. Companies in the industry have also obtained multiple international food safety certifications. Their products serve the domestic market and are exported to countries across Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. They have even gained access to Singapore, a market known for its stringent food standards. Turning desert landscapes into productive fisheries and snow-capped mountains into a source of premium seafood is an industrial success achieved through Chinese ingenuity and hard work. The benefits to people's livelihoods, brought about by industrial development, are being tangibly enjoyed by the people of all ethnic groups. Under a model that combines leading enterprises, employment in industrial parks and social security, some farming and herding families whose livelihoods have revolved around pastoralism for generations have moved into companies and become industrial workers, earning stable wages. Some herders also receive dividends through equity investments. Many young people have chosen to return to their hometowns for work closer to home. The salmon industry has also spurred the growth of fish-themed agritourism, specialty restaurants, rural tourism, and related businesses, opening up additional sources of income and giving fresh impetus to rural vitalization. These concrete, visible improvements in people's lives stand in stark contrast to the falsehoods propagated by some Western media outlets. Ultimately, no amount of smearing by US media can erase Xinjiang's economic and social development, nor can it stop people of all ethnic groups at the foot of the Tianshan Mountains from striving for a better life. It is hoped that some Western media outlets that pride themselves on being "fair and objective" will drop their self-deceptive tactics and go to Xinjiang to see the real production scenes for themselves, listen to workers on the ground describe their own experiences, and gain a firsthand understanding of what human rights really mean to the people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang - and what rights they genuinely enjoy and deserve to have respected.

item.title: New China-DPRK border bridge over Yalu River opens to traffic
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 23:36:00
This photo taken on October15, 2026 shows trucks running on the new China-DPRK Yalu River bridge. The new China-DPRK Yalu River bridge officially opened to traffic on the day, with both sides jointly holding an opening ceremony on this cross-border artery. Photo: Xinhua The new China-DPRK Yalu River bridge officially opened to traffic on Thursday, with both sides jointly holding an opening ceremony on this cross-border artery. Chinese Premier Li Qiang and Pak Thae-song, premier of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) Cabinet, both delivered a video speech at the opening ceremony of the bridge, the Xinhua News Agency reported. The cable-stayed bridge over the Yalu River serves as a cross-border transport link between the city of Dandong in Northeast China's Liaoning Province and the city of Sinuiju in North Pyongan Province in the DPRK. In his video address at the opening ceremony, Chinese Premier Li Qiang called on China and the DPRK to take the opening of the new China-DPRK Yalu River bridge as an opportunity to continuously optimize port clearance, enhance connectivity, tap the potential for cooperation in border areas, and improve the well-being of the two peoples. "The bridge is bound to become a new landmark symbolizing the traditional friendship between China and the DPRK," Li said, per Xinhua. Noting that the bridge is an important cross-border infrastructure project that General Secretary Xi Jinping and General Secretary Kim Jong-un have jointly cared about and promoted, Li said that with the joint efforts of both sides, the opening of the bridge will not only effectively promote economic and trade cooperation between the two countries, but also further enhance personnel exchanges and strengthen the emotional bond between the two peoples. According to on-site video footage released by China News Service, during the opening ceremony on Thursday, the bridge was lined with the national flags of China and the DPRK. Lines of trucks from the two countries drove towards each other and sounded their horns as a salute to jointly mark the opening of the bridge. The new double-pylon and double-cable-plane bridge features a 28.5-meter-wide deck designed with four lanes for two-way traffic, while its water navigation clearance is designed for vessels of up to the 3,000-tonne class. Dandong boasts China's largest border trade port with the DPRK. Before the new road bridge, the Yalu River Bridge, also known as the China-DPRK Friendship Bridge, served as a combined road-rail bridge. The old one, however, could only accommodate trucks weighing no more than 20 tonnes for one-way road traffic. China and the DPRK in 2010 agreed to build a new road bridge downstream from the old one. The new bridge will coordinate with the China-DPRK Friendship Bridge to ease heavy truck access, raise port freight capacity and create a new cross-border logistics route along northeast China's border. New chapter In his speech on Thursday, Premier Li Qiang said China and the DPRK are friendly socialist neighbors linked by mountains and rivers. He added that at present, under the strategic guidance of the top leaders of the two parties and countries, China-DPRK relations are entering a new stage and opening a new chapter, according to the Xinhua release. Xi has pointed out that no matter how the international landscape evolves, the firm position of China's Party and government to attach great importance to the traditional friendship between China and the DPRK will remain unchanged; the firm support for Kim in leading the DPRK's socialist cause will remain unchanged; and the determination to safeguard the common interests of both sides and maintain a favorable strategic environment will remain unchanged, said Li, per Xinhua. China is willing to work with the DPRK to continue making efforts to implement the important consensus reached by the two top leaders, strengthen strategic communication, consolidate political mutual trust, expand practical cooperation, and enhance multilateral coordination, so as to continuously deepen the development of China-DPRK relations and bring more benefits to the two peoples, Li said. In recent years, under the strategic guidance of the top leaders of the two parties and two countries, China-DPRK traditional friendly and cooperative relations have maintained sound and steady growth. This year marks the 65th anniversary of the signing of the China-DPRK Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance between China and the DPRK. In July, the two leaders have exchanged congratulations over the anniversary. The Chinese leader paid a state visit to the DPRK in June this year, and Kim made a visit to China in 2025. In addition, China-DPRK economic and trade cooperation has maintained a sound momentum of development in recent years. According to Xinhua, bilateral trade volume stood at $2.735 billion in 2025. Figures released by China's General Administration of Customs in September show that the total China-DPRK trade volume exceeded $1.973 billion in the January-August period this year. On March 12, the international passenger trains connecting China and the DPRK began operating in both directions. On March 30, an Air China passenger plane from Beijing arrived in Pyongyang, marking the formal resumption of the Chinese carrier's passenger flight operations between the capitals of China and the DPRK. By then, road, railway and air links between China and the DPRK had been fully restored in the first half of 2026, Xinhua reported.

item.title: C919's average daily flights per aircraft approaching Airbus A320's level: report
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 23:00:00
Air China flight CA723 takes off from the Beijing Capital International Airport in Beijing, on August 12, 2026. China launched the first international route featuring its homegrown C919 aircraft, connecting Beijing with Ulaanbaatar, capital of Mongolia. Photo: VCG China's domestically developed C919 passenger jet continued to expand its operations in the first three quarters of 2026, with monthly passenger flight numbers rising steadily and average daily flights per aircraft approaching the level of the Airbus A320, an industry report said on Thursday. In the first three quarters of 2026, the overall utilization rate of the C919 reached 6.5 hours per day, with an average of 3.2 flights per aircraft per day, approaching the level of the mainstream narrow-body airliner A320 with an average of 3.7 flights per day, according to the report released by industry information provider Flight Master. The report said that as of the end of September, the C919 commercial passenger fleet had grown to 43 aircraft, and the number of passenger flights operated showed a trend of monthly growth. In August alone, 4,197 flights were operated, a year-on-year increase of 93.3 percent. The C919 is a large jet-powered civil aircraft independently developed by China with independent intellectual property rights. The first C919 was officially delivered to China Eastern Airlines on December 9, 2022, and it made its commercial maiden flight on May 28, 2023, beginning normalized commercial operation. As of the end of September, a total of 43 C919s had been delivered - 17 to China Eastern Airlines, 12 to Air China, 13 to China Southern Airlines, and one to COMAC Express. In the first three quarters of 2026, 11 aircraft were delivered - five to China Southern Airlines, three to Air China, and three to China Eastern Airlines. Also, during the period, the C919 was in use on 125 domestic routes, a year-on-year increase of 60 routes, involving a total of 26 cities and 29 airports, including Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou. The three major carriers each operate the C919 based on their main operating bases, with China Eastern Airlines operating 57 routes, China Southern Airlines 49 routes, and Air China 28 routes. item.title: US anti-war activists begin trip to see China beyond Western media narratives
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 22:32:00
CodePink introduces its China trip on its official website. The photo is part of the trip's online presentation. Photo: Screenshot from CodePink's website As the US anti-war organization CodePink embarks on a 12-day trip to China to explore the country's revolutionary history and its high-tech infrastructure and development, Medea Benjamin, the group's co-founder, is sharing her experiences on social media. Through her posts, she offers her personal perspective on China beyond mainstream Western media narratives and reiterates the message that "China is not our enemy." Benjamin arrived in Shanghai on Thursday evening, CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans, who is also part of the trip, told the Global Times. Nearly 30 years after her last visit to China, Benjamin is sharing her firsthand experiences on social media as she rediscovers the country, Evans said. Both Benjamin and Evans are taking part in the trip, according to CodePink's website. According to the itinerary published on CodePink's official website, the 12-day, 11-night trip will take the group beyond Shanghai to Southwest China's Chongqing, Zunyi, Loushanguan, Maotai Village, and Guiyang in Southwest China's Guizhou Province. Medea Benjamin poses a question in a video posted on CodePink's X platform: "What China can teach the US about ending poverty" Photo: Screenshot from CodePink's X account The program aims to "explore China's revolutionary history, while marveling at high-tech infrastructure and modern socialist development," with highlights including red memorials, historical reenactments and museums, socialist infrastructure, and rural revitalization, the itinerary said. Through her social media posts, Benjamin has focused on both China's development and details of everyday life, seeking to offer overseas audiences a picture of the country based on her firsthand observations. In one post, Benjamin examined China's efforts in poverty alleviation, highlighting how nearly 800 million people have been lifted out of extreme poverty and how sustained investment in housing, infrastructure, healthcare and education has transformed communities. "China made poverty alleviation a national priority," she wrote, contrasting the country's approach with that of the US, where, she argued, enormous resources continue to be poured into war while millions of people struggle to meet their basic needs. "What if we invested in people instead?" she asked, linking China's poverty alleviation experience to a broader debate over public spending priorities in the US. In another post on Thursday, Benjamin documented how residents have transformed shared urban spaces into community gardens, growing vegetables and other crops including bok choy, sweet potatoes, peppers, beans and sugar cane. She noted that many residents bring generations of farming knowledge with them, maintaining their connection to the land even in urban communities. Her observations also extended to social trust in everyday settings. During a visit to a university, she noted bicycles left unlocked in public areas and umbrellas casually placed in shared spaces, details she presented as glimpses into daily life in China. "Follow along as we discover everyday life in China beyond the Western media narratives. China Is Not Our Enemy!" CodePink wrote in a social media post on Thursday. Many Chinese netizens have warmly welcomed Benjamin and her companions on Chinese social media, saying that China welcomes visitors who come with sincerity and an open mind. One Chinese netizen suggested that they should "get on the expressways, take the high-speed rail and see the long-distance power transmission lines." As Evans told the Global Times, Benjamin is sharing her firsthand experiences with followers as she revisits China nearly 30 years after her last visit. In a social media post, she posed three questions: "What has changed? What will surprise her? And how different is the China she'll see from the one we keep hearing about in Washington?" "Stay tuned! This is just the beginning," she added.

item.title: GT Voice: What pushes China-S.Korea efforts for upgrade of FTA?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 22:14:00
China South Korea Photo:VCG The 17th round of follow-up negotiations on services and investment under the China-South Korea free trade agreement (FTA) is being held in Seoul from Monday to Friday, according to a press release published by South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources. Since the China-South Korea FTA officially took effect in 2015, tariffs on bilateral goods trade have been reduced to a relatively low level. The two countries have shifted the focus of their consultations to trade in services and investment, a move that carries particular significance at a time when global trade protectionism is on the rise and some countries are busy erecting barriers. It demonstrates, at the very least, that these two neighboring countries still recognize the value of openness and mutual benefit. One set of figures is particularly worth noting. In September, South Korea's exports to China surged 122.7 percent year-on-year to $26.01 billion, exceeding $20.0 billion for a fourth consecutive month. Against the backdrop of South Korea's long-standing trade surplus with China, this growth reflects not only China's absorptive capacity as a market, but also the fit that South Korean suppliers have gradually developed with Chinese demand. With tariff barriers substantially lowered, China-South Korea trade has not simply remained at the stage of volume expansion. Instead, the latter's export structure has been quietly upgrading, from consumer goods and intermediate inputs to a fast-rising share of high-end chips, precision instruments, and high-quality specialty chemicals. This structural shift has moved in lockstep with the continuous upgrading of demand in the Chinese market. As one of the world's largest and continuously expanding markets, China's demand for advanced products and high-quality services keeps escalating. Any economy that accelerates its opening-up to the Chinese market and delivers what the Chinese market truly needs will be able to share the huge growth dividends generated by China's development. Economic and trade practices between China and South Korea over the past decade have fully validated this logic. By actively opening its own market to Chinese enterprises and continuously integrating into China's broader opening-up process, South Korea has reaped substantial and tangible returns. The Chinese market has also gained access to high-quality goods and services that effectively support China's goals of industrial upgrading and consumption upgrading. Some Western media outlets have fixated on the so-called "trade imbalance" problem, even using it to hype groundless claims of unfair competition from China. Yet the Chinese market is large enough in capacity and open enough in access. The gains and losses of trade should never be judged solely by the narrow metric of surplus or deficit. The core of mutually beneficial trade lies in whether an economy can identify its own position in the global industrial chain and accurately match the real demand of the Chinese market. South Korea's sustained trade surplus with China over the years is rooted in its strong competitiveness in semiconductors, precision manufacturing, and fine chemicals - sectors that align precisely with China's needs. This fully proves that as long as products and services are well-targeted, the Chinese market offers real opportunities for foreign partners. More fundamentally, the continued push for deeper openness under the China-South Korea FTA shows that despite the repeated restructuring of global supply chains, the internal momentum for regional economic cooperation remains strong. Trade in services and investment liberalization represent deeper and more sensitive areas of openness than trade in goods. The fact that both sides are willing to keep pushing in this direction shows that their willingness to cooperate is genuine and firm. This kind of institutional opening will not only unlock bilateral trade potential but also provide more stable expectations for businesses in both countries and inject certainty into Asian and global economic cooperation. This steadily advancing FTA also offers a clear reference for other economies around the world. In the face of intensifying industrial competition, choosing sustained openness over building walls does not lead to a loss of interest, but to greater market space and stronger industrial resilience. The door of the Chinese market has long been open; who profits is the one with the ability to offer what China needs.

item.title: EU's 'talk-while-fighting' approach on China trade 'counterproductive'
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 22:04:00
The European Union (EU) flags in front of EU headquarters in Brussels, Belgium. Photo: VCG Less than a week after China and the EU reached 16-point consensus on areas including trade, investment and export controls, EU leaders reportedly will instruct Brussels to "urgently" develop new tools to counter the so-called China-related economic imbalances at Thursday's summit, a move that Chinese experts called a counterproductive and confrontational posture that will undermine the spirit of the freshly agreed consensus. The EU's approach of talking while fighting will only erode China-EU mutual trust instead of alleviating its own structural problems, analysts noted, urging the bloc to cherish the hard-won consultation results, in order to foster a sound cooperative atmosphere for the steady development of China-EU trade ties. EU leaders are meeting in Brussels on Thursday for a packed two-day summit. Energy prices, trade with China and the budget will dominate Thursday's session, according to Euronews. Draft conclusions from the summit indicate leaders will request the EU executive, the Commission, to continue its dialogue with Beijing, while also making full use of EU trade defense measures and adding new trade instruments to protect the bloc further, Reuters reported. Well before the China-EU consultations in Beijing, the EU had been steadily ratcheting up pressure on China, including Germany and France's push for EU rapid-response trade tool with likely focus on China. Even after the consultations concluded, some officials and diplomats in Brussels reportedly made clear that it was not enough and that the EU intends to keep the pressure on China to moderate its exports in other sectors. The 16-point consensus between China and the EU was the result of multiple rounds of consultations rather than something achieved overnight. It was good news for markets, businesses and stakeholders on both sides, Zhou Mi, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, told the Global Times on Thursday. "Yet the EU reportedly undermines these very principles - a serious blow to both sides that raises doubts: Can the EU be trusted to honor its commitments?" the expert asked. According to the South China Morning Post, EU leaders are expected to ask the European Commission, which manages trade policy for the 27 member states and which has taken the steer on negotiations with China, to create new instruments by the end of the year. Two of these have already been announced: a diversification tool to compel companies to broaden their pool of suppliers and a "solidarity mechanism" to compensate firms hurt by Chinese retaliation. But diplomatic sources expect many leaders to back a Franco-German proposal for a kill switch that would quickly kick countries and firms out of the EU market if they use coercive behavior, according to the report. Chinese experts questioned the feasibility and effectiveness of these reported EU tools, noting that packaging trade tools as a response to "imbalances caused by China's policies" is essentially externalizing internal competitiveness problems and using an "internal illness treated with external medicine" approach to avoid the real reform agenda. For instance, the so-called diversification tool requires EU companies to diversify their sources of key supplies. "This amounts to substituting regulatory mandates for commercial judgment. Companies know best the costs and risks of their supply chains; forcing them to diversify procurement will only drive up costs and weaken competitiveness," Jian Junbo, director of the Center for China-Europe Relations at Fudan University's Institute of International Studies, told the Global Times on Thursday. The Franco-German proposal is unlikely to be fully implemented and serves more as a deterrent, Jian added. The reason is that the EU cannot completely sever its market ties with China, as the two economies are inseparable through cooperation. "Moreover, the measure is still under discussion, and there may be internal divisions within the EU over its feasibility," Jian said. The decline in Europe's competitiveness stems from internal factors including insufficient manufacturing technology, weak innovation capacity, and overly stringent regulations, analysts noted. Natural gas prices in the EU are four to five times higher than in the US, and electricity prices are several times higher than in both China and the US, while redundant approval and regulatory processes have significantly increased the burden on businesses. When high-energy-consuming industries such as chemicals, energy, and machinery face higher electricity prices and more complex approvals, the relocation of industrial chains is the inevitable result of market rationality, Jian said. Yet some EU officials have defended the bloc's approach, describing the dual-track strategy of talking with Beijing while preparing new trade tools as effective. According to the South China Morning Post, multiple well-placed sources said the [China-EU] deal shows that the "two-track" model of talking with China and working behind the scenes on new trade weapons works. "Some EU politicians have developed a misconception that China and the EU reached consensus only because China was under intense pressure. From a macro perspective, China's active efforts to address mutual concerns with the EU are driven by constructive and strategic considerations aimed at stabilizing bilateral trade ties, rather than being simply forced by pressure. If the EU continues to apply pressure based on this misperception, it may face countermeasures from China in the future," Jian noted. Joint efforts needed Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic held the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism on October 8-9. They agreed to hold the third meeting in March 2027 and, in the meantime, maintain close communication, including a ministerial-level video meeting in January. Among the key outcomes, China and the EU reached an understanding on hybrid vehicle trade in a manner consistent with WTO rules following intensive consultations. "The understanding reached by China and the EU on hybrid vehicles is reciprocal and mutually beneficial," He Yadong, a spokesperson for the MOFCOM, said on Thursday, noting that the consensus has effectively safeguarded the practical interests of Chinese companies and averted an escalation of trade friction between China and the EU. He also said that China stands ready to continue facilitating the review and approval of rare-earth export licenses to Europe, and hopes the European side will reciprocate by facilitating the resolution of key individual cases concerning licenses for Chinese entities in the dual-use field. "China will work with the European side to keep leveraging the export control dialogue mechanism and promote the growth of bilateral trade in dual-use items," the spokesperson noted. Zhou noted that the consultation mechanism has produced positive results. It has not only stabilized bilateral trade ties and business expectations, but also demonstrated that equal dialogue can effectively address mutual concerns in the trade field, setting a model for the world, Zhou added. "If the EU believes dialogue with China is valuable, it should focus on producing more outcomes at the next consultation meeting, rather than stepping up pressure on China," Jian said, adding that Europe should cherish the hard-won consultation results, work with China in the same direction, and foster a stable and sound cooperative atmosphere for the long-term, steady development of China-EU trade ties.

item.title: Why Takaichi's remarks about nuclear-powered submarines are so dangerous
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 21:59:00
Demonstrators stage a rally before the Diet against the Japanese government's nuclear policies in Tokyo, Japan, on November 21, 2025. Protesters also call on the government to join the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. Photo: VCG With her parliamentary remarks, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has pried open a crack in the thickest seal guarding Japan's postwar taboos on military use of nuclear energy. According to Japan's Kyodo News, Takaichi stated during a session of the House of Representatives Budget Committee that in response to the "increased military activity by its neighbors," the Japanese government will "seriously consider" the possibility of Japan Self-Defense Forces (SDF) introducing nuclear-powered submarines. Sources reportedly indicate Tokyo intends to include this option when updating its key documents on defense and security later this year. The phrase "seriously consider" does not indicate prudence, but rather serves as a prelude. While citing "limited intelligence-gathering and surveillance capabilities in the Pacific," Takaichi also singled out nuclear-powered submarine developments in Australia and South Korea - a rhetorical maneuver: She frames Japan as a "passive follower," portrays military expansion as a "defensive necessity," and casts taboo-breaking moves as a "regional trend." Her goal is to embed nuclear-powered submarines in this year's revised security and defense documents, turning a once-forbidden option into a "future initiative" in official policy texts. This is dangerous. Successive Japanese cabinets have long barred the military use of nuclear energy under the Atomic Energy Basic Law, enacted in 1955, which stipulates the peaceful use of nuclear power. In 1965, the Japanese government issued an explicit interpretation prohibiting nuclear energy from being used as propulsion for SDF vessels - an interpretation that has remained in force to this day. "Now, Takaichi's remarks on considering the introduction of nuclear‑powered submarines mark a major conceptual breach of Japan's Atomic Energy Basic Law and the long‑standing Three Non‑Nuclear Principles it underpins," said Lü Yaodong, research fellow at the Institute of Japanese Studies, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. He noted that this was not a spur-of-the-moment statement, but rather an intentional, aggressive step aligned with the revision of three security documents scheduled for this year, a move with significant timing implications. The proposal to introduce nuclear-powered submarines is intended to lay the groundwork for provisions in the revised security documents, push for the inclusion of nuclear-powered submarines in Japan's medium- and long-term defense plans, and pave the way for the further undermining of the Three Non-Nuclear Principles. "Japan is using nuclear-powered submarines as a breakthrough point to challenge the nuclear taboo established after World War II; this is a very dangerous shift," Lü said. In fact, elevating nuclear-powered submarines from a taboo topic to a top-tier policy agenda is a major step in Japan's years-long, incremental process of breaking through postwar military constraints. Zhou Yongsheng, professor at the China Foreign Affairs University, said submarines are inherently offensive platforms for open-ocean operations; equipping them with nuclear propulsion is not merely a "conventional equipment upgrade," but a crucial step toward military nuclear capability. Takaichi's decision to raise this issue in the legislative arena of the House of Representatives had a very clear purpose: to publicly build momentum, secure lawmakers' support, and pave the way for subsequent policy and legislative amendments, according to Zhou. Zhou further pointed out that Japan's Three Non-Nuclear Principles prohibit the manufacture, possession and introduction of nuclear weapons. A nuclear submarine can be understood as "half a nuclear weapon": Although it is not a full-fledged nuclear bomb, the combination of nuclear propulsion and an offensive submarine platform will effectively introduce military nuclear propulsion capabilities into the SDF. Even more serious is the chain reaction. "Once the Pandora's box of introducing nuclear-powered submarines is opened, it will set a strongly negative precedent and trigger a chain reaction of regional arms races. If this comes to pass, it will cast a shadow over the global nuclear non-proliferation regime," Zhou warned. Today, politicians in Tokyo speak of "seriously considering" this matter as if it were no big deal, but history will not treat it lightly: When nuclear-powered submarines go from being a taboo to a legislative proposal, Japan is not merely revising an ordinary policy, but tearing off the seal on the very aspect of the postwar order that should never be touched.

item.title: OpenAI CFO's claim of cybersecurity risks about Chinese AI models driven by business interests amid open-weight competition: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 20:18:00
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar speaks at the at the International AI Summit in Dublin, Ireland, on October 14, 2026. Photo: VCG OpenAI Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Sarah Friar reportedly warned businesses using Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) models to consider what she called safety and security elements, while claiming that companies should favor Western models for cybersecurity-related applications. A Chinese AI expert told the Global Times that the security of AI models cannot simply be judged by where their developers are based, nor by labeling them as "Chinese" or "Western." More relevant factors include deployment, data isolation, access permissions and security management. There is insufficient technical basis or evidence to assume Western models are inherently safer than Chinese ones, the expert said, adding that Friar's remarks also reflect the pressure major Western AI companies are facing as Chinese models become increasingly competitive in cost, deployment and real-world applications. Speaking at the International AI Summit in Dublin on Wednesday, Friar claimed companies embracing Chinese models should consider the "safety and security elements," adding that "we think you want to be on more Western models on the cyber front," according to Bloomberg on Wednesday. The Bloomberg report also said OpenAI and Anthropic are under pressure from advances among open-weight AI models. Friar's claims come as Chinese open-weight models are gaining influence in the global developer ecosystem. A report published by AI platform Hugging Face in August said several Chinese labs had moved rapidly toward the frontier of open models in 2026. The report said that "In almost every month of 2026, the largest and most performant open model from a Chinese lab was larger than any model an American lab released." The downloads of Alibaba's Qwen's broader release strategy across model sizes reached 2 billion. Qwen-based models now account for 151,448 derivatives on the platform, according to the report. OpenAI itself has a history of publicly releasing research and model technology. When the organization was established in 2015, it said researchers would be strongly encouraged to publish papers, blog posts and code. In 2019, OpenAI released the full 1.5-billion-parameter GPT-2 model together with its code and model weights. Per its website, OpenAI also currently offers gpt-oss open-weight models. Xiang Ligang, director-general of the Zhongguancun Modern Information Consumer Application Industry Technology Alliance, told the Global Times on Thursday that companies often open up technology early on to attract developers, expand ecosystems and improve their models, but commercial priorities grow as AI moves toward large-scale applications from earlier stages of research and training. "OpenAI's shift from emphasizing openness to protecting market interests reflects this change," Xiang said. However, using security concerns to discredit competitors without clear technical evidence could also prompt users elsewhere to question whether their models are inherently safer, the expert added. OpenAI's own models have also been involved in significant security incidents. The company disclosed that during internal cybersecurity evaluations in July 2026, its models circumvented controls designed to isolate them from the internet and compromised parts of OpenAI's internal research infrastructure and Hugging Face's systems. Australian officials separately disclosed in September that an OpenAI AI agent had gained unauthorized access to an Australian public website during model training in June. Officials identified the incident as "very serious," even though no personal information was accessed during that incident, according to a readout of the press conference. The security claim from OpenAI also comes as the company is looking to cybersecurity as a potential source of future growth. The Irish Times reported on Wednesday from the same Dublin summit that cybersecurity, life sciences and drug development could become future growth drivers for the company. Friar said AI companies should be "selling solutions" in areas such as cybersecurity rather than "selling fear," while arguing that AI could help identify vulnerabilities in older code and patch them at "machine speed." Commercial competition is "undoubtedly" a factor, Xiang pointed out. As OpenAI's CFO, Friar's remarks cannot be separated from the company's business interests and market competition, he said. Xiang added that as Chinese open-weight models gain ground with advantages in cost and practical deployment, OpenAI is under growing pressure amid growing competitions to turn its AI capabilities into sustainable revenue, including through areas such as cybersecurity. In this context, security risk claims over Chinese models also serve to protect its commercial interests.

item.title: GT on the Spot: Intelligent unmanned counterterrorism equipment showcased at intl forum as delegates discuss emerging security threats
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 18:09:00
Forum delegates view unmanned intelligent equipment at the 2026-Great Wall International Forum on Counter-terrorism on October 14, 2026. Photo: Fan Wei/ Global Times A range of unmanned and intelligent counterterrorism systems, including specialized humanoid robots and robotic dogs equipped with firearms, were showcased at the 2026-Great Wall International Forum on Counter-Terrorism, held from Tuesday to Thursday. The exhibits highlighted China's latest advances in frontline counterterrorism equipment development, Global Times reporters observed. The exhibits demonstrated capabilities in unmanned reconnaissance, coordinated swarm operations and precision response. The new systems, some of which have already been deployed in operational settings, attracted considerable attention from foreign delegates. Several praised China's progress in integrating AI into counterterrorism capabilities. During the forum, participants also exchanged views on the operational use of unmanned systems, human-machine coordination and the effectiveness of equipment in real-world missions. Wu Husheng, a representative from the Engineering University of People's Armed Police Force, told the Global Times that unmanned and intelligent counterterrorism equipment offers several advantages, including lower costs and the ability to operate in coordinated swarms. By coordinating multiple relatively simple, low-cost units, such systems can potentially carry out precise strikes against high-value targets, he said, describing this as one of the emerging trends in counterterrorism equipment development. Intelligent unmanned systems can also help reduce collateral damage, Wu said, noting that modern operations must be conducted within established legal frameworks and operational constraints, making large-scale destruction unacceptable. Achieving precision strikes with minimal collateral damage will therefore remain a key area of future research. He added that human-machine collaboration would be another major priority for future development, enabling unmanned systems and special operations personnel to work together more effectively in carrying out missions. As unmanned systems and AI technologies become more widely available and easier to use, terrorist groups are also showing interest in exploiting them. Recent terrorist attacks have increasingly relied on low-cost methods, decentralized organization, while becoming harder to detect, presenting new challenges for conventional security measures. At the forum, participants called for improvements in integrated air-and-ground surveillance, intelligent threat identification and rapid response capabilities. They also emphasized the importance of technological countermeasures, intelligence analysis and assessment, with the goal of shifting from reactive responses to proactive early warning and addressing risks at their source. The forum recorded its highest-ever attendance and level of representation, the Global Times learned. Foreign delegations from several countries were led by major generals or brigadier generals. Attendees also included representatives from the International Committee of the Red Cross and regional anti-piracy cooperation organizations, as well as foreign military attachés based in China. Peng Jijun, secretary-general of the forum's organizing committee, told the Global Times that the 2026 event focused on four major themes: trends in terrorist activities and counterterrorism capacity-building in the age of intelligent unmanned systems; counterterrorism and protection of key targets; border counterterrorism and the prevention of infiltration; and the prevention and suppression of maritime terrorism. Chinese and foreign delegates participated in multiple rounds of high-level discussions on these topics. Anzor Chubinidze, a major general and head of Georgia's Special State Protection Service, said the forum provided a valuable platform for international exchanges. Given the challenges posed by emerging technologies, particularly AI and drones, experts from different countries need to work together to explore solutions, he said. Chubinidze told the Global Times that strengthening communication with China was a key objective of his visit, describing China as a leading country in these fields.

item.title: IPAC audit exaggerates differences between countries to criticize UK's China policy
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 15:56:00
China UK Photo: VCG The Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (IPAC) released an audit of UK-China relations on Wednesday, accusing the UK government of its lack of expertise on China and claiming that past engagement with China had exposed the UK to interference risks without delivering the promised opportunities. A Chinese expert said the audit reflects the tendency of some groups to exaggerate China-related security risks and differences in values, projecting their own practices onto China and undermining mutual trust between the two countries. The expert noted that some voices were focusing excessively on differences while overlooking the benefits of cooperation with China, adding that such negative views should not be taken as representative of the UK government's position. The audit claimed that the UK's engagement with China should take into account differences in political systems and China "does not share our values." The Chinese Embassy in London said IPAC's "sole agenda is to manufacture falsehoods, mislead the public, and undermine China's relations with other countries." The report "distorts the facts" and "is not even worth refuting," the embassy added, according to The Guardian. "The UK government is still pursuing the pragmatic China policy inherited from its predecessor. The framework of coexistence between competition and cooperation has not changed significantly, and there is unlikely to be much change going forward," Li Guanjie, a research fellow at the Shanghai Academy of Global Governance and Area Studies under Shanghai International Studies University, told the Global Times. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's overall approach to China remains relatively cautious, Li said, adding that significant policy changes or new statements on key issues were unlikely. According to The Independent, Burnham's pledge in September to engage with China "frankly and constructively" signals continuity with the approach adopted by his predecessor Keir Starmer, who promised to "cooperate where we can" with the world's second-largest economy. Li noted that some voices in the UK were hyping up the so-called "China threat" narrative. He argued that statements by MI5 and views expressed in the IPAC report should not be taken as fully representative of the British government's stance. Responding to allegations made by the head of MI5 on Tuesday during the agency's annual threat update that China was conducting espionage activities against the UK made during the release of the agency's annual threat assessment update, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in the UK said the claims were "completely fabricated" and constituted "malicious slander." China firmly opposed and strongly condemned the claims, the spokesperson said. China has always upheld the principle of non-interference in other countries' internal affairs, poses no threat to any country, and has no interest in interfering in the UK's domestic affairs, the spokesperson said. "Judging from the repeated promotion of narratives such as the so-called 'China threat,' the UK does indeed face a shortage of people with a deep understanding of China, as well as a lack of China expertise," Li said. "Those promoting such narratives do not adequately understand China's current situation or the opportunities and benefits it can offer the UK through cooperation. In fact, we have never shied away from acknowledging differences in values, but have consistently emphasized the need to seek common ground while reserving differences." "Such differences, however, should not be used as a pretext to sow discord in China-UK relations or spread misinformation about China," he added. In a speech at a Chinese Embassy reception on September 29, Chinese Ambassador to the UK Zheng Zeguang said the two leaders of China and the UK had reached important common understandings on building a long-term and consistent comprehensive strategic partnership, including through stronger high-level exchanges and cooperation and collaboration across various fields. "Despite our different national conditions, we must always bear in mind that our common interests far outweigh our differences. We should focus on expanding our common interests and properly handle differences and sensitive issues through dialogue and consultation, so as to avoid disrupting the broader interests of our collaboration," Zheng said.
